title: The £5.5B Sizewell C deal and the RAB gamble
narrative_md:
**Britain is betting that if it builds another Hinkley Point, but funds it through consumer bills this time, it won't cost twice as much.**

On 30 July 2024 the new Labour government confirmed a £5.5 billion commitment to Sizewell C — the Suffolk nuclear plant that will, if built, supply 7% of UK electricity. The deal relies on an untested funding model, RAB, and a simple bet: that bill-payers can be charged during construction more cheaply than contractors can borrow.

Sizewell C has been a decade in the political queue. The original project agreement, signed by Theresa May's government in 2013 as Hinkley Point C's sister plant, used the same Contract-for-Difference model — no public risk, no bill-payer surcharge during construction, but a guaranteed strike price of £92.50/MWh (2012 prices) for 35 years after commissioning. Hinkley's costs have since doubled from £18 billion to £46 billion; EDF absorbs the overrun, but the strike price means consumers overpay for decades.

The Regulated Asset Base model, legislated for in the Nuclear Energy (Financing) Act 2022, works differently. Bill-payers start contributing a few pounds a year from construction start, probably 2027, rising to tens of pounds at peak. In return, the headline cost of capital drops — the Treasury's central estimate is that RAB saves £30 billion-plus across the plant's life versus CfD financing. The gamble is that the political system can sustain visible surcharges on household bills for a decade before a single kilowatt-hour is generated.

The geopolitics changed the cast. China General Nuclear Power, the original 20% equity partner, was forced out in November 2022 after the National Security and Investment Act 2021 gave ministers new powers to block infrastructure ownership. The Treasury bought CGN out for £679 million and has been seeking replacement private equity since. In July 2024 Labour committed a further £5.5 billion alongside EDF's reduced stake, with Final Investment Decision targeted for mid-2025.

The delivery vehicle is Sizewell C (Holding) Limited, currently wholly owned by DESNZ but structured to take private equity. The Low Carbon Contracts Company, which holds all UK CfDs, will contract with Sizewell C for the post-commissioning period. The RAB regulator is Ofgem.

Critics make three arguments. First, no RAB model has ever financed nuclear anywhere in the world — Finland's Olkiluoto ran 14 years late on a different model. Second, bill-payer surcharges are a regressive tax: every household pays equally, regardless of income. Third, the assumption that Sizewell C avoids Hinkley's delays relies on design replication — but every EPR built so far has been bespoke.

Defenders argue that without nuclear baseload, the UK cannot hit Net Zero by 2050 with the renewables-plus-gas mix currently deployed. The 2035 coal phase-out, hitting in September 2024, has tightened winter margins. Offshore wind growth has slowed. The gap has to be filled.

If Sizewell C comes in on-budget at £20-24 billion and on-time for 2035, RAB will be vindicated. If it becomes another Hinkley, British households will be paying for it on their bills through the 2040s.
